query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a nanolayered architecture into the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy via the incorporation of ultrathin graphene interlayers will arrest crack propagation and boost mechanical integrity without disturbing its intrinsic caloric phase transition.
generation.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 produced as a bulk high‐entropy alloy that shows a large caloric response under applied field/pressure but suffers from poor toughness and cracking.
generation.intervention: Process the alloy into a nanolaminated composite structure that alternates thin layers (on the order of 5–10 nm) of the high‐entropy alloy with monolayer (or few‐layer) graphene.
generation.conditions: Under operational conditions involving applied magnetic and/or pressure fields over the intended temperature range, as well as moderate cyclic mechanical loads typical in device applications.
generation.structural_mediator: The periodic graphene interlayers act as ‘crack arresters’ by deflecting and bridging crack tips and redistributing local stresses.
generation.mechanism: Graphene’s exceptionally high strength and stiffness, when integrated as ultrathin, coherent interfaces, will inhibit the propagation of microcracks in the brittle-prone alloy while its minimal volume fraction preserves the bulk’s caloric transition behavior. This interfacial reinforcement is expected to enhance compressive or flexural strength without diluting the phase transformation responsible for the caloric response.
generation.predicted_outcome: The nanolaminated (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38/graphene composite should exhibit significantly improved mechanical integrity (e.g., higher fracture toughness and compressive strength compared to epoxy-containing or liquid-metal composites) while maintaining a caloric response (entropy change and adiabatic temperature change) close to that of the unmodified alloy.
generation.baseline: The current bulk (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy displays excellent caloric performance but poor structural integrity due to its propensity to crack.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be beneficial when the graphene layer thickness remains ultrathin (e.g., below ~10 nm) and its total volume fraction is low enough so as not to kinetically hinder the phase transition that yields the caloric effect; extreme deformation conditions beyond typical device loadings have not been considered.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis builds on findings from studies of nanolayered CoCrFeNi/graphene composites (e.g., PMC9227879 and PMC11469235 evidence) that demonstrate crack-arresting effects of graphene interfaces. It extrapolates these benefits to an MM′X alloy system (here, the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy) and assumes that the ultrathin graphene layers will not disrupt the caloric phase transition. The precise influence on the transformation kinetics remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 processed as a conventional bulk material and a second set processed into nanolaminated composites with ultrathin graphene interlayers. Subject both sets to cyclic mechanical testing under applied magnetic/pressure fields while simultaneously measuring their caloric responses (e.g., entropy change, adiabatic temperature change). Use microstructural characterization (SEM/TEM) to assess crack propagation.
measurements: Mechanical properties (compressive strength, fracture toughness, cyclic durability)
Caloric effect metrics (magnetocaloric/barocaloric entropy change and temperature change)
Microstructural analysis (crack initiation and propagation at graphene interfaces)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the graphene-interlayered samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in mechanical integrity (e.g., crack resistance or compressive strength) compared to the baseline, or if their caloric performance is significantly diminished relative to the unmodified alloy, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: We showed here that a non‐equiatomic FeCoNiTaAl HEA system can be turned into a material with a good property profile of strength, ductility and soft magnetic response, by introducing homogeneously distributed coherent and ordered nanoprecipitates. The formation of these nanoprecipitates is due to the strong interaction among Al‐Ta and Al‐Ni, respectively, which promotes the formation of intermetallic phases with some solid solution variation on the sublattices. The good combination of strength and ductility derives from massive solid solution, nanoprecipitation and dynamic microband strengthening, yielding mechanical features beyond those reported before for soft magnetic materials. The full coherency of the ordered nanoprecipitates and the matrix contributes significantly to the strength with only a slight increase in coercivity. The alloy design concept opens a pathway for developing novel soft magnetic materials with improved mechanical properties, such as needed for the electrification of industry and transportation.

As for the fracture behaviors, i.e., the early crack generated in HEA film, the crux of the problem lies in the high aspect ratio of HEA grains, as experimentally proved by the SEM and TEM observations. The CoCrFeNi HEA films populated with columnar grains suffer from easier buckling events in terms of Euler’s criterion [,]. Particularly, a larger aspect ratio sustains stronger cohesive strength of grain boundaries to block buckling. In such a condition, columnar grains tend to buckle and prompt the entire structure to lose its load-bearing limit, and, consequently, the fracture comes about the individual grain boundary cracking. Heavy nanotwins embedded in the nano-sized grains of the HEAs are suggested to accommodate the dislocation motion and cater to the further plastic deformation and delay the crack propagation []. More importantly, the experimental observation on crack features indicated that the monolayer graphene interface can strongly hinder and arrest crack propagation.
